sections.heading: Key points
sections.content:
*   Emerging technology may be this era's existential crisis, as many people feel a loss of autonomy.
*   Much like the anxiety of the Cold War era, the AI era has produced a societal sense of worry.
*   Counterbalancing worry with optimism can help navigate the uncertainties of advancing technology.

In a May 2026 survey conducted by the American Psychological Association, more than half of the participants identified “the impact of emerging technology in everyday life” as an issue they were somewhat or very anxious about (APA, 2026). The seemingly unstoppable emergence of [Artificial Intelligence](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/artificial-intelligence "Psychology Today looks at Artificial Intelligence") (AI) seems to be driving this rise in tech-related [anxiety](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/anxiety "Psychology Today looks at anxiety"), so much so that recently a new psychological concept, “AI Anxiety,” has begun to appear in scholarly articles and research. Advancing technology, which was once viewed as a mainly positive development that could improve our lives, is beginning to be seen more as an existential threat that could lead to our downfall. According to the Pew Research Center, concern about AI now heavily outweighs excitement, with a jump from 31% of respondents feeling concerned to 55% since 2021 (McClain & Park, 2026).

sections.heading: Evolving Societal Concerns
sections.content: Over time, societal concerns evolve and change, and our collective psychology evolves along with these broader changes. For example, in psychology texts from the midcentury, worries about the Cold War, nuclear annihilation, and the atomic bomb were often referenced as the main anxieties of the period. According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), “the political and military tension between the U.S. and the Soviet Union fostered a profound anxiety in our nation during the 1950s,” driven by “the atomic explosions at Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945…[and] the horrors of nuclear warfare” (Moore & Moore, 2009). While there remains an underlying societal anxiety about war and nuclear capability, these fears seem much less tangible than they perhaps did in the 1950s and have been replaced by fears related to loss of autonomy due to rapidly advancing technology.

sections.heading: The Loss of Autonomy
sections.content:
In a 2024 article, Johannessen et al. point out that people typically want to control their own [decision-making](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/decision-making "Psychology Today looks at decision-making") process; however, rapidly advancing technology and AI often cause us to feel that we are losing our ability to control this process and that our [free will](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/free-will "Psychology Today looks at free will") and autonomy are being directly threatened. In response to this, the European Commission passed into law an Artificial [Intelligence](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/intelligence "Psychology Today looks at Intelligence") Act that requires medical AI to have “explainability,” which can be enhanced with “causability” to promote better understanding of the rationale underlying AI decisions (Plass et al., 2023). In other words, the European Union now requires that AI have a greater level of transparency, particularly for high-risk AI systems, such as those that are used in healthcare. In the United States, however, no such sweeping guideline or law has been passed, and AI continues to evolve and grow without specific regulations. An article in the _Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology_ describes AI as having its own autonomy, “which means AI is out of human control, thus there is concern that AI may autonomously harm human beings” (Johnson & Verdicchio, 2017). This threat to personal autonomy and decision-making can cause significant anxiety.

sections.heading: The Existential Threat
sections.content: We might view the current realities about emerging and advancing technology as this era’s existential threat, much like the nuclear annihilation worries of the midcentury. According to the APA, existential anxiety is characterized by “angst associated with one’s freedom as a human being to make choices” (APA, 2026). In my private practice, I currently work with multiple clients in the tech industry who feel concerned that AI will eliminate their jobs and that there is not much they can do to prevent it. This is not necessarily an irrational [fear](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/fear "Psychology Today looks at fear") that has no basis, much as fears of nuclear war in the 1950s were not necessarily irrational either. When existential worry becomes rampant, feelings of hopelessness and helplessness can result, yet another blow to our sense of personal autonomy.

sections.heading: Counterbalancing Worry
sections.content:
In the 1950s, despite the looming possibilities of negative outcomes related to nuclear capability, people did continue to live their lives—they had families, worked, went about their daily business, and engaged in their lives. Midcentury psychologist and author Rollo May wrote of the strange duality of a sky that at once could be expansive and beautiful but was also the place from which an atomic bomb could fall. In a sense, we are living in a similar reality: the advancement of technology has produced countless benefits, yet it comes with great risk at the same time. May’s point was that it was worth seeing the sky as beautiful every now and then rather than as a constant, impending threat.

In practical terms, this counterbalancing of two distinct realities might take the form of engaging less with technology, connecting more with your present life, relationships, and self-care, and recognizing that there will always be a societal threat, no matter the era. From there, we can find a collective will to cope rather than to give in to existential fears. Sanae Okamoto, a psychologist and behavioral scientist at the United Nations University–Maastricht Economic and Social Research Institute on [Innovation](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/creativity "Psychology Today looks at Innovation") and Technology in the Netherlands, reminds us that “we’re all in this challenge together” and that confronting AI anxiety begins with “building solidarity, finding community and coming up with collective solutions” (Leffer, 2023). Indeed, finding ways to counterbalance our worry with collectiveness and solidarity can help us navigate a time in history that will undoubtedly be written about in many psychological texts, just as the Cold War era was.

## Much like midcentury concerns about nuclear war, technology is today's anxiety.

### Key points

*   Emerging technology may be this era's existential crisis, as many people feel a loss of autonomy.
*   Much like the anxiety of the Cold War era, the AI era has produced a societal sense of worry.
*   Counterbalancing worry with optimism can help navigate the uncertainties of advancing technology.

In a May 2026 survey conducted by the American Psychological Association, more than half of the participants identified “the impact of emerging technology in everyday life” as an issue they were somewhat or very anxious about (APA, 2026). The seemingly unstoppable emergence of [Artificial Intelligence](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/artificial-intelligence "Psychology Today looks at Artificial Intelligence") (AI) seems to be driving this rise in tech-related [anxiety](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/anxiety "Psychology Today looks at anxiety"), so much so that recently a new psychological concept, “AI Anxiety,” has begun to appear in scholarly articles and research. Advancing technology, which was once viewed as a mainly positive development that could improve our lives, is beginning to be seen more as an existential threat that could lead to our downfall. According to the Pew Research Center, concern about AI now heavily outweighs excitement, with a jump from 31% of respondents feeling concerned to 55% since 2021 (McClain & Park, 2026).

## Evolving Societal Concerns

Over time, societal concerns evolve and change, and our collective psychology evolves along with these broader changes. For example, in psychology texts from the midcentury, worries about the Cold War, nuclear annihilation, and the atomic bomb were often referenced as the main anxieties of the period. According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), “the political and military tension between the U.S. and the Soviet Union fostered a profound anxiety in our nation during the 1950s,” driven by “the atomic explosions at Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945…[and] the horrors of nuclear warfare” (Moore & Moore, 2009). While there remains an underlying societal anxiety about war and nuclear capability, these fears seem much less tangible than they perhaps did in the 1950s and have been replaced by fears related to loss of autonomy due to rapidly advancing technology.

## The Loss of Autonomy

In a 2024 article, Johannessen et al. point out that people typically want to control their own [decision-making](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/decision-making "Psychology Today looks at decision-making") process; however, rapidly advancing technology and AI often cause us to feel that we are losing our ability to control this process and that our [free will](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/free-will "Psychology Today looks at free will") and autonomy are being directly threatened. In response to this, the European Commission passed into law an Artificial [Intelligence](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/intelligence "Psychology Today looks at Intelligence") Act that requires medical AI to have “explainability,” which can be enhanced with “causability” to promote better understanding of the rationale underlying AI decisions (Plass et al., 2023). In other words, the European Union now requires that AI have a greater level of transparency, particularly for high-risk AI systems, such as those that are used in healthcare. In the United States, however, no such sweeping guideline or law has been passed, and AI continues to evolve and grow without specific regulations. An article in the _Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology_ describes AI as having its own autonomy, “which means AI is out of human control, thus there is concern that AI may autonomously harm human beings” (Johnson & Verdicchio, 2017). This threat to personal autonomy and decision-making can cause significant anxiety.

## The Existential Threat

We might view the current realities about emerging and advancing technology as this era’s existential threat, much like the nuclear annihilation worries of the midcentury. According to the APA, existential anxiety is characterized by “angst associated with one’s freedom as a human being to make choices” (APA, 2026). In my private practice, I currently work with multiple clients in the tech industry who feel concerned that AI will eliminate their jobs and that there is not much they can do to prevent it. This is not necessarily an irrational [fear](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/fear "Psychology Today looks at fear") that has no basis, much as fears of nuclear war in the 1950s were not necessarily irrational either. When existential worry becomes rampant, feelings of hopelessness and helplessness can result, yet another blow to our sense of personal autonomy.

## Counterbalancing Worry

In the 1950s, despite the looming possibilities of negative outcomes related to nuclear capability, people did continue to live their lives—they had families, worked, went about their daily business, and engaged in their lives. Midcentury psychologist and author Rollo May wrote of the strange duality of a sky that at once could be expansive and beautiful but was also the place from which an atomic bomb could fall. In a sense, we are living in a similar reality: the advancement of technology has produced countless benefits, yet it comes with great risk at the same time. May’s point was that it was worth seeing the sky as beautiful every now and then rather than as a constant, impending threat.

In practical terms, this counterbalancing of two distinct realities might take the form of engaging less with technology, connecting more with your present life, relationships, and self-care, and recognizing that there will always be a societal threat, no matter the era. From there, we can find a collective will to cope rather than to give in to existential fears. Sanae Okamoto, a psychologist and behavioral scientist at the United Nations University–Maastricht Economic and Social Research Institute on [Innovation](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/creativity "Psychology Today looks at Innovation") and Technology in the Netherlands, reminds us that “we’re all in this challenge together” and that confronting AI anxiety begins with “building solidarity, finding community and coming up with collective solutions” (Leffer, 2023). Indeed, finding ways to counterbalance our worry with collectiveness and solidarity can help us navigate a time in history that will undoubtedly be written about in many psychological texts, just as the Cold War era was.
